Comparison

TPO vs. PVC: Which Welded Membrane?

The two hot-air-welded single-ply membranes compared on fixed criteria — chemical resistance, track record, cost, and the building conditions that decide between them.

Source verification in progress Updated July 15, 2026 2 min read Editorial standards · Report an error
Source verification in progressSources for this page are still being verified. Details may change.

Key takeaways

  • Both weld into monolithic surfaces; the choice is about exposure and premium, not seam quality.
  • Grease, chemicals, or industrial exhaust on the roof → PVC. No such exposure → TPO usually wins on price.
  • PVC's field history is longer; TPO's formulations have converged upward but vary more by manufacturer.
  • Specify thickness and attachment identically before comparing any bids.

How this comparison was built

Fixed criteria applied identically, per the CRI Methodology: service life, seams, chemical exposure, fire, cost, track record, and best-fit conditions. Sources are standards and technical data, not marketing.

Side by side

CriterionTPOPVC
Typical service life15–25 years20–30 years
SeamsHot-air weldedHot-air welded
Grease/chemical resistanceLimitedHigh
Field track record~30 years50+ years
Formulation consistencyVaries by manufacturerMore standardized
Typical cost positionLowerPremium
Late-life repairabilityGoodHarder (brittleness)

What actually decides it

  • Restaurant / food service / industrial exhaust: PVC, full stop. Grease degrades TPO and can void its warranty.
  • Standard office, warehouse, retail with clean exposure: TPO’s price advantage usually holds; PVC’s premium buys resistance the roof will never use.
  • Owner risk posture: the longest welded-membrane history is PVC’s. Owners who pay for track record are buying something real, if rarely decisive.
  • Cold-weather installation: PVC generally welds more forgivingly in marginal temperatures — an installation-quality consideration, not a performance one.

Common mistakes

  1. Comparing a 45-mil TPO bid against a 60-mil PVC bid and calling PVC “expensive.”
  2. Putting TPO over a kitchen exhaust field to save the premium — then losing the warranty argument later.
  3. Treating all TPO as identical; manufacturer formulation history matters more in TPO than in any other membrane. Ask for the specific product’s field history.

FAQ

Is KEE membrane the same as PVC? KEE (Ketone Ethylene Ester) membranes are a related thermoplastic with plasticizer stability advantages — worth pricing on harsh-exposure roofs; typically a further premium.

Can PVC and TPO be repaired with each other’s material? No — they are not weld-compatible. Repairs must match the membrane chemistry.
